EICMA 2026 • Honda CRF1150L Africa Twin Enduro Sports Is a Tongue Twister, Weighs Less but Offers More
Ford F-150 Raptor R Meets All-Time Rival Ram 1500 SRT TRX. Which Is the Fastest Truck?
11 photos
Photo: Hennessey Performance | YouTube
The Ram 1500 SRT TRX and the Ford F-150 Raptor R are the two fastest and most powerful factory-production, gas-powered pickup trucks on the market. So every time they meet, sparks come out of their third-degree encounter. This time, Hennessey Performance got them on its proving ground to see which one is faster.
It would normally all come down to numbers. The all-new Ram 1500 SRT TRX has 57 horsepower more, so they should both pack their things and go home. However, while things are clear on paper, they might not be as clear on the track.
The Ford F-150 Raptor R has the ferocious 5.2-liter Predator V8 with supercharged firepower under the hood. The Predator roars out 720 horsepower (730 metric horsepower) and 640 pound-feet (868 Newton meters) of torque.
Those are enough to make it rocket from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 3.6 seconds, run the quarter mile in 12.0 seconds with a trap speed of 113 mph (182 kph), and max out at 114 mph (183 kph), which is electronically governed since the truck rides on massive 37-inch off-road tires. The V8 has to pull a truck that tips the scales at 5,950 pounds (2,699 kilograms).
Photo: Hennessey Performance | YouTube In the meantime, Stellantis, with new leadership after Carlos Tavares’s abrupt departure in December 2024, brought back part of what its former CEO had chosen to pull the plug on. It is basically the return of the prodigal son by popular demand.
The Ram 1500 SRT TRX is powered by the almighty 6.2-liter supercharged HEMI V8, which pumps out 777 horsepower (788 metric horsepower) and 680 pound-feet (922 Newton meters) of torque, which is more than what the F-150 Raptor R can do, no matter how you look at it.
The TRX is slightly quicker from 0 to 60, taking 3.5 seconds for the run, but a bit slower down the quarter mile with 12.2 seconds and a trap speed of 114 mph (183 kph) on its way to a top speed of 118 mph (190 kph), electronically limited for the same reason as its counterpart. The HEMI-powered truck is also heavier at 6,294 pounds (2,885 kilograms).
Alex and Adam from Hennessey Performance brought the two out on the track to determine the absolute king of the hill in the ICE-powered performance truck segment. The truck war takes place at Hennessey’s Pennzoil Proving Ground test track in Sealy, Texas.
Photo: Hennessey Performance | YouTube While the TRX wants to show that it is back with a bang after a three-year hiatus, the Raptor R intends to prove it is here to stay. Alex will be driving the Ram, while Adam will have to deal with the Ford-badged truck.
On the first pass, the two trucks launch like rockets, squatting and nearly throwing the front axle nearly going up in the air. The Ford takes a fragile lead, but it is a short-lived glory, because the Ram eventually gains momentum and wins. That is because it hits the speed limit at 113 mph.
On a roll race, both in Sport mode, the F-150 Raptor once again seems faster. This time, it keeps the lead all the way to the end before Adam and Alex move off the track and into the rough terrain for a high-speed pass.
Both trucks feature the off-road mode, specifically engineered for off-road driving and high-speed desert running. The two get off the line like no tomorrow, with a trail of dust following close behind. The winner takes it all, and that is the Ram. No surprise there. Despite the extra weight, it’s got the extra oomph to compensate.

EICMA 2026 • 2027 Suzuki SV-7S Unveiled at the EICMA Show in Italy: I’m Suddenly More Nostalgic Than Ever
The Tourne Select Is a High-End Camper Van for Anyone Who Wants Comfort Without the Show
16 photos
Photo: Tourne Campervans
What we have here is a conversion based on a brand-new Fiat Ducato model. Tourne Campervans, based in Pivka, Slovenia, is the company behind this project. It specializes in custom-fitted, all-season-ready camper vans.
After I wrote about Tourne's newest camper van addition, the Expre, I was curious to see what other builds the company offers.
The Select is available in two versions, a 6-meter one and a 6.4-meter one – the only difference is the way you sleep. The shorter version has a crosswise sleeping arrangement, while the longer one has a lengthwise arrangement.
According to its maker, the Tourne Select is fitted out for maximum comfort, performance, and flexibility. Let's see if that's the case, starting, as always, with the exterior.
Tourne shared that it doesn't want the Select to stand out or scream "camper van," but still pack quality features. I'd say it managed to do that, with the rig not screaming camper van as in it will not grab too much attention.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Campervans That said, it's quite obvious, at least to someone who's seen a camper van before, that the Select is a tiny home on wheels, even though it doesn't have that many upgrades.
The van rides on black alloy wheels wrapped in all-terrain tires. On top, you'll come across solar panels and a large awning. Other notable mods are power and water hook-ups and a compartment that lets you access the toilet from the outside.
Enter, and a bright interior will greet you. It has an open layout, with no wall separating the driver's cabin from the living space. What's more, the driver and passenger seats are mounted on swivel bases that allow you to turn them around to face the back of the van.
Regarding aesthetics, you'll notice laminated cabinetry with a light grain finish, black flooring, and white walls with a matching ceiling. Most of the furniture is created in-house from wood and hand-assembled in the company's shop.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Campervans Straight ahead as you enter, you'll discover a seating area. It comprises a dual bench seat and a table, with a large overhead cabinet above. The seating area has Tourne's patented bed system called the Dream4.
Long story short, you can use slide-outs and several panels that come together like puzzle pieces to transform the seating area into a bed that can sleep two kids or even two adults if they don't mind a snug fit.
Next, we have the kitchen on the passenger side, by the entrance. It features a deep black stainless steel sink with a cover, a portable single-burner induction stove, and a tall 78-liter Thetford fridge with a tiny freezer compartment.
A spice rack, a lower cabinet with adjustable shelves, several drawers, and a sizeable overhead cabinet are available for storage. One of the drawers doubles as a slide-out countertop, as it has a removable top.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Campervans Of course, a deluxe camper van like the Select will offer one of the most sought-after amenities in a home on wheels: a bathroom, hidden behind a white retractable door. It boasts a toilet, a skylight that can be opened, and a small corner sink with a pull-out faucet that can double as a showerhead.
A distinctive touch in the bathroom is that the toilet is mounted on a swivel base so you can turn it around to use it and turn it back to create more space when unused. Moreover, the bathroom can double as a drying area, as it has a vent pumping hot air.
The rear part of the interior is taken up by a large bedroom. Even though it's not fully divided from the rest of the living space, the bedroom does feel like a separate room because of the kitchen and bathroom wall panels that partly close it off. The bedroom also offers two large overhead cabinets, two shelves, and charging points.
Tourne Campervans came up with a clever setup to be able to utilize the space in the back. The bed platform is made up of three panels that can be raised and strapped to the cabinets on the driver's side.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Campervans Two boxes on the sides hold the bed platform panels, offer extra storage space, and accommodate the utility systems.
Power is on the left side – unfortunately, we don't know the exact battery capacity, but we do know that it's enough to sustain off-grid travel.
As for plumbing, the van is equipped with a heated 90-liter (23-gallon) freshwater tank above the passenger-side wheel well and a heated and insulated 100-liter (26-gallon) greywater tank underneath the van.
Traveling in colder environments is not an issue in this rig, as it sports not one but two heaters. The first is a Truma Combi heater that offers both hot water and heated air, while also powering a heated floor system. The second is a Webasto diesel-powered air heater.
Photo: YouTube Screenshot / Tourne Campervans The control panel for the rig's utilities is conveniently located above the entrance. It includes a touchscreen display that lets you monitor and control the power system and a digital thermostat for the Truma heater.
All in all, the Tourne Select creates ideal home-like conditions for you on the road, letting you go off-grid in comfort and style. There's one more thing to mention, one that makes the camper van an even more attractive offering: the price.
The starting price of the Select is £84,507 ($112,774) for the 6-meter version or £86,607 ($115,577) for the 6.4-meter one. To be fair, these are the prices I managed to find from last year – it's best to check in with the company for updated information.

EICMA 2026 • Honda Has a Taste of the e-MTB World with the RN0 Motor-Assisted Bicycle
Jay Leno Rides Shotgun in the 1938 Delahaye 165 Cabriolet, the Car Flooded in a Container in 1953
21 photos
Photo: Audrain Museum Network | YouTube
This 1938 Delahaye 165 Cabriolet has been riding the waves of automotive history. Literally. It got flooded with salt water while being shipped in an open container in the early 1950s, it was painted green, then restored to its original red. Now, two months after it won the First in Class award at the Pebble Beach Concours d’Elegance, where it was also a Best of Show nominee, it hits the road with its owner in the driver's seat and Jay Leno riding shotgun.
The owner of this motorized beauty is Fritz Burkard, a car collector coming from the Swiss Alps and in love with the sea. That is why, driving his 1938 Delahaye 165 Cabriolet along the coast of the Atlantic, with the top down, makes him cheer and raise his fist in joy. " The sea is something special ," he says from the driver’s seat, with Jay Leno sitting right beside him.
The first time Fritz Burkard saw the car completely restored was before the Pebble Beach Tour at six o’clock on Thursday morning. It was August 13, the day the Pebble Beach Tour d'Elegance took place, preceding the main Concours d'Elegance Sunday.
The car had belonged to Anne and Robert Lee before it was acquired by prominent collector Chip Patterson. He was the one who sold it to Fritz Burkard in 2021 and sent it straight to RM Auto Restoration in Canada for a frame-off overhaul. The restoration took exactly five years to complete.
Photo: Audrain Museum Network | YouTube The 1938 Delahaye 165 Cabriolet is the absolute peak example of French Art Deco "rolling sculpture". Combining the high-performance engineering of a Grand Prix racer with coachwork by Figoni et Falaschi, it is widely considered one of the most beautiful and exclusive automobiles ever created.
It may look better than it did when it first saw the light of day back in 1938, in time for that year’s Paris Motor Show, but it has had its fair share of turbulence. After spending the immediate post-war years being driven and raced in Europe, it was purchased by an American importer and shipped across the Atlantic.
It was during this 1953 voyage that the vessel was battered by an Atlantic storm. The open container that was supposed to protect it, secured on the deck of the cargo ship, couldn’t keep the waves away, so it filled with the destructive saltwater that ruined the original V12 engine. Actually, all internals suffered severe corrosion damage.
The car was rendered entirely non-running, and the original engine was eventually separated from the chassis and sold off in Germany. The rolling chassis ended up with a dealer in Fresno, California. But it was so bad that it had to be put through era-specific restoration immediately. The car was fitted with a Cadillac V8 engine that replaced the destroyed V12, along with a new automatic transmission.
Photo: Audrain Museum Network | YouTube To make it road-legal and fit the American styling trends of the time, it was painted dark green and fitted with heavy, clunky chrome bumpers that entirely ruined the original Figoni et Falaschi’s delicate teardrop silhouette.
It took decades and massive financial resources from the Robert Lee family and then the meticulous five-year-long frame-off restoration for Fritz Burkard to completely erase the scars of the disastrous saltwater and return the car to its former glory from 1938.
The 1938 Delahaye 165 Cabriolet was built on a road-adapted version of the legendary Type 145 racing chassis with aluminum body panels shaped over a tubular steel frame. Only two examples were ever constructed with this specific, sweeping Figoni cabriolet bodywork. The original engine, the one that was the victim of saltwater, was a 4.5-liter 60-degree aluminum V12 derived from Delahaye’s Grand Prix racing program.
The V12 puts out 245 horsepower through the rear wheels with the help of the innovative Cotal electromagnetic gearbox. This engineering marvel of the pre-war era acts like a semi-automatic. Instead of using mechanical shift linkages and synchros to slide gears into place, the Cotal system uses electromagnets to engage different planetary gear sets inside the transmission.
Photo: Audrain Museum Network | YouTube While accelerating in a gear, the driver moves the tiny lever into the slot for the next gear. Nothing happens immediately. The gear is simply pre-selected. To complete the gear change, the driver simply lifts their foot off the accelerator, and the electrical circuit cuts over, the magnets instantly switch, and the new gear engages with no need for the driver to touch the clutch pedal.
This example's sister car was shipped to America to represent France at the 1939 New York World's Fair. Because of WWII's outbreak, it became stranded in U.S. Customs for six years, was sold, spent years fitted with a Cadillac V8 engine, and was eventually purchased by Peter Mullin for the Mullin Automotive Museum.
Following the closure of Mullin's museum , it was transferred to the Petersen Automotive Museum in Los Angeles. The two cars recently reunited in person for the very first time at the Petersen Museum. While the 1939 example lives a pampered museum life, the 1938 unit continues to rack up awards.
It was a First in Class and Best of Show finalist at the 2026 Pebble Beach Concours and won the Best of Show at the 2026 Audrain Newport Concours. Now, it has hit the roads of Rhode Island with Fritz Burkard in the driver’s seat and Jay Leno as his trusty co-driver.

EICMA 2026 • Triumph TF-E Bikes Get Even More Enduro With Updates for the 2027 Model Year
ABT RSQ8-LE 1000 Is a Monstrous Audi RS Q8 With 1,000 Horsepower
8 photos
Photo: Instagram | abt_sportsline
ABT Sportsline has been on a roll recently, as it unveiled several cool projects, including that Audi RS 5 Avant that we covered last week.
More recently, the famous tuner has pulled the wraps off another interesting build. It is called the ABT RSQ8-LE 1000, and as mentioned in the title, it is a monstrous Audi RS Q8 with a four-digit output. We kid you not, this machine is roughly as punchy as the original Bugatti Veyron, which is the world’s first hypercar, and it remains a family-friendly machine and a very good daily.
The tuner says that the Audi RS Q8 in question has the ABT Power R performance upgrade, complete with a new turbo, an intercooler, a water/ethanol injection system, and other upgrades. The result? A massive 1,000 horsepower. The output is actually in metric horsepower, and it translates to b986 rake horsepower and 736 kilowatts. The top speed has been increased to a more exotic figure of 199 mph (320 kph).
How does it compare to the standard model? With no outside intervention, the RS Q8 has 640 ps (631 hp/571 kW), and that’s 360 ps (355 hp/265 kW) less than the ABT RSQ8-LE 1000. The twin-turbocharged 4.0-liter V8 engine produces 850 Nm (627 lb-ft) of torque. It’s unknown how fast the tuned crossover coupe is, but the standard one hits 60 mph (97 kph) in 3.4 seconds. Flat-out, it does 155 mph (250 kph), and this number increases to 190 mph (305 kph) when ticking the RS Dynamic Package Plus box on the options list.
Photo: Instagram | abt_sportsline The vehicle also features the ABT Body Control System, which is an adaptive roll stabilization system, for a more engaged driving experience. A stainless steel exhaust system with four tailpipes, each one measuring 105 mm (4.1 in) in diameter, is also on deck, enhancing the car’s soundtrack. The model rides on ABT’s High Performance IR23 FlowForming wheels, 23 inches in diameter, which were wrapped in 295/35 tires. The alloys were painted gold, and the body is presented in green.
Moreover, the ABT RSQ8-LE 1000 also features enhanced aerodynamics. The novelties include the splitter, front skirt and hood inserts, wheelhouse ventilation at the front, door mirror casings, and B-pillar covers. The fender extensions, door strip attachments, rear skirt add-ons, rear skirt inserts, and wing with aero blades have also come from ABT Sportsline’s portfolio, and some of them have a matte carbon look.
The changes continue on the inside, where the steering wheel, which was wrapped in Alcantara, and the shift paddles, shift knob cover, dashboard covers, and seat frame covers in matte carbon, are mentioned. Other highlights include the dedicated door sills, a special logo on the center console, a new start-stop switch cap, ABT and RSQ8-LE logos on the seats, floor mats with embroidered RSQ8-LE logos, and trunk mat.
ABT’s RSQ8-LE 1000 represents the final chapter in the tuner’s trilogy, and it is capped at only 30 units worldwide. The tuner’s Instagram post embedded at the bottom of the page does not mention the pricing, but its official website does. And in order to turn your Audi RS Q8 into the ABT RSQ8-LE 1000, you will have to spend 165,000 euros overseas. This equals a little over $185,000 at the current exchange rate.
Photo: Instagram | abt_sportsline Mind you, that does not include the installation, which is another 20,000 euros (~$22,500), including tax, so you are looking at 185,000 euros ($207,850) in total. And no, that does not include the donor vehicle. As for the complete vehicle, you will have to spend a whopping 345,000 euros (equal to $387,610). And that’s Lamborghini Urus SE Performante territory, though between us, the ABT RSQ8-LE 1000 will smoke it all day, any day.
The Audi RS Q8’s Italian cousin has 812 ps (801 hp597 kW) combined from its plug-in hybrid 4-liter twin-turbocharged V8 and 1,000 Nm (738 lb-ft) of torque, taking 3.3 seconds to hit 100 kph (62 mph), and maxing out at 312 kph (194 mph). The Urus SE Performante has an electric driving range of 60 kilometers or 37 miles.
A brand new Audi RS Q8 Performance will set you back a minimum of $139,700 (equal to 124,325 euros) in the United States of America for the 2027 model year, and it kicks off at 146,200 euros ($164,255) for the regular RS Q8 and 160,000 euros ($179,760) for the RS Q8 Performance in its homeland of Germany.
Now, if you found yourself sitting on almost $400K and you wanted a cool super crossover for daily duties, would you really blow that much money on the ABT RSQ8-LE 1000? That’s a tricky one, as while it will smoke not only the Lamborghini Urus, which is based on the same platform, but also the Ferrari Purosangue and the Aston Martin DBX, but in the end, it is still an Audi, albeit one that carries an extremely exotic price tag. Server
Server Systems
Dell PowerEdge R770AP Front 1
The Dell PowerEdge R770AP is a 2U air-cooled, dual-socket server known for its high core density. It supports up to two Intel Xeon 6980P processors, each with 128 cores, for 256 installed cores total. Given the current Diamond Rapids schedule, this is set to be the major Intel platform for some time. We had been hoping to try this with Intel’s Xeon 6+ Clearwater Forest but Intel could not get us chips. The -AP stands for “Advanced Performance,” at least for the Intel ecosystem. Dell made a really sweet Intel Xeon server built around flexible I/O and storage. We wanted to get this review up with our newer AgentSTH V7 benchmarks, so let us get to it.
Dell PowerEdge R770AP External Hardware Overview
Starting from the outside, the R770AP presents as a standard 2U rack chassis with an 801mm rear I/O depth without bezel per Dell’s current technical specifications. The front of the system is dominated by storage, but not in the way you might expect from previous generations.
Dell PowerEdge R770AP front panel showing two E3.S drive banks flanking central ventilation section
Before we go too far, note that we have one configuration, but Dell offers many options for storage and expansion. So please take this more as an example configuration, but you can spend a lot of time in Dell’s configurator customizing these.
Angled view of Dell PowerEdge R770AP front placing E3.S banks and central intake in whole chassis context
On the front lower edge, we get the Dell R770AP model markings and the service tag. You would be surprised by how many server models out there actually do not have the model number printed and visible from the front. One small impact is that the drive bays are labeled 25-31 with an arrow because the service tag replaces the area where the drive numbering would normally be printed.
Close-up of Dell PowerEdge R770AP model marking at front lower edge
The front panel splits into two banks of E3.S carriers that are separated by a central ventilation section. The left and right banks each hold vertically oriented E3.S carriers with orange release markings that make individual drives easy to identify and remove.
Vertical E3.S carrier bank on Dell PowerEdge R770AP with orange release markers and printed bay numbers
Having the center area dedicated for airflow on previous-generation 2.5″ drive bay servers meant you would usually have fewer than 24 possible U.2 drive bays up front. With E3.S, you get both a direct air channel in the center, as well as 32x E3.S drive bays with 16x on either side.
Straight-on close view of numbered vertical E3.S carriers on Dell PowerEdge R770AP front
Our configuration uses four Dell DC NVMe CD8P E3.S MU 1.6TB SSDs. Dell’s current product specifications list front storage options including up to 32x EDSFF E3.S Gen5 NVMe drives, an alternative with up to 16x 2.5-inch U.2 Gen5 x4 or x2 NVMe SSDs, and a no-backplane option. The E3.S form factor allows more devices per chassis than the 2.5-inch option. You can see the Kioxia CD8 1.6TB E3.S SSD here.
Removed Dell DC NVMe CD8P E3.S MU 1.6TB SSD from the PowerEdge R770AP
An E3.S carrier is smaller than a U.2 carrier, which helps with density but makes the latches slimmer.
Released E3.S carrier angled out from Dell PowerEdge R770AP front bank showing access mechanism
The right front ear houses a power button, information status control, and a USB Type-C socket.
Dell PowerEdge R770AP right front ear with power button, USB Type-C and information/status control
Dell specifies this connector as USB 2.0 Type-C, so do not get too excited about a Thunderbolt-capable Type-C port on a server. We have a few servers now, however, that are using Type-C for data and video as their local KVM I/O, so perhaps that will be where that goes one day, but this is more of a service port.
Close-up of front USB 2.0 Type-C port and info/power buttons on Dell PowerEdge R770AP
On the top, we get a normal Dell latching top which is smooth, but also expected since it is a dell.
Full side view of Dell PowerEdge R770AP chassis showing rail mounting features
On the sides, we get sheet metal since this is meant to connect to rails.
Opposite side view of Dell PowerEdge R770AP chassis with mounting features
Dell’s rails for this are also super easy to install.
Rack slider assemblies supplied for the Dell PowerEdge R770AP shown beside server
The rear panel layout places riser modules across the top and power supplies at the lower sides. A modular boot network group and management ports occupy the central space between these.
Complete rear panel view of Dell PowerEdge R770AP showing riser slots, PSUs and modular I/O group
You might be wondering about that big metal bit sticking out. That is a handle that Dell has been offering for generations. As the servers get bigger and heavier, the handle becomes more useful.
Rear angled whole chassis view of Dell PowerEdge R770AP with module depth and handles visible
The power supplies here are redundant 1.8kW units. Dell has many different power supply options, so this is just what we are using for this server.
Dell PowerEdge R770AP Hot Swap Power Supply 4
Below the risers, Dell groups the fixed rear I/O in an arrangement that has become familiar across recent PowerEdge generations. You get VGA for local console access, two USB Type-A ports that Dell specifies as USB 3.1, and a dedicated iDRAC Ethernet port for out-of-band management.
Dell PowerEdge R770AP rear VGA, dual USB Type-A ports and dedicated iDRAC Ethernet below risers
A dedicated iDRAC Ethernet RJ45 socket sits next to the rear USB and VGA ports. This provides a separate physical connection for out-of-band management access, distinct from standard data networking interfaces. This iDRAC interface has been around for so long that it is one of the names people use for all out-of-band management solutions.
Closeup of dedicated iDRAC RJ45 management port on Dell PowerEdge R770AP rear
We also get two rear USB 3.1 ports for local keyboards, mice, and USB storage.
Two blue rear USB 3.1 Type-A sockets on Dell PowerEdge R770AP
The VGA connector provides the analog console path that many data center operators still rely on for initial bring-up or emergency access. Many data centers use VGA carts. That is funny, since we have servers now well into the five-figure range for a dual-socket server, yet shared $200 monitors on data center carts keep us using this analog technology.
Rear VGA connector close-up for local console access on Dell PowerEdge R770AP
The Dell BOSS-N1 DC-MHS boot solution sits at the rear. Our unit carries two 480GB M.2 NVMe drives behind little orange release levers. Aside from BOSS being a cool brand name, it also provides a RAID 1 OS solution for those who are using OSes like VMware or Windows Server, where you may need some sort of non-software RAID for a boot volume. Here, Dell also saves two of the front bays by using the BOSS option in the back.
Dell BOSS-N1 DC-MHS boot module with two 480GB M.2 NVMe carriers and orange release levers at rear of R770AP
Dell uses OCP NIC 3.0 cards for primary networking in the back so you can get low-speed RJ45 networking or high-speed 200Gbps+ ports. This system configuration has both Broadcom BCM57608 and ConnectX-6 Dx controllers installed.
Lower rear network module labeled Port1/Port2 with two cages on Dell PowerEdge R770AP
On the rear, Dell has many riser configurations, so it is more of a pick-your-own adventure in terms of full-height, low-profile, and other configurations. In server designs, fitting today’s higher-power NICs, DPUs, GPUs, and more in the rear requires significant thermal design effort because the SSDs, CPUs, and memory heat the air before it reaches the rear risers.
Upper rear network cage positions next to Gen5 labeling on Dell PowerEdge R770AP
In this generation, many will use lower-speed 10G and 25G networking. We have QSFP56 networking here for 200Gbps ports. With this generation of Xeon 6, you can easily run 400Gbps NICs (1x 400G or 2x 200G).
